what: StoneX Group is a financial services firm that helps companies, institutions and individuals trade commodities, currencies and securities. It clears futures, makes markets in bonds and equities, deals in precious metals and handles global payments.
customers: Commodity producers and users, hedge funds, banks, brokers and retail traders worldwide.
money: Hedging and trading for commodity producers and users.
Clearing, market making and fixed income for institutions.
Retail trading platforms and cross-border payments.
moat: A rare combination of commodity expertise, clearing licences and global reach in a niche that big banks have left.
risks: Reported revenue is huge ($162B) because physical metals trades are booked at full value; it says little about profit.
Cash flow swings with client balances, so it is not a useful guide.
Market volatility drives earnings, which can fall in quiet markets.
opportunities: Net income grew from $116M in 2021 to $525M over the last twelve months.
At about 9 times earnings, it is cheaply valued.
Higher interest rates boost earnings on client balances.
Acquisitions such as R.J. O’Brien add scale.
watch: Net operating revenue growth and interest income on client funds.
view: StoneX’s reported revenue of $162 billion and its volatile cash flow are both misleading: physical metal trades are booked at full value, and client balances move cash in and out. The useful number is profit, which has grown more than fourfold since 2021 to $525 million over the last twelve months.

At about 9 times earnings, the market prices it like a cyclical trading firm whose profits depend on volatility and interest rates. That is partly fair, but StoneX has grown steadily by adding clients and buying competitors.
This turns on interest rates and market activity. I think the shares are cheap for a business with this growth record, though earnings will dip if rates fall sharply and markets calm down.
bull: Client growth and acquisitions keep earnings rising even as rates fall.
bear: Lower rates and quieter markets cut earnings sharply.
